correctness.rationale: The first cut removes only its named vertex and meets its incident exchange edges at their other endpoints. Any new edge lies in the product-of-simplices cut facet. At an adjacent second deleted vertex its product neighbors are also single exchanges, so the second cut again creates no fractional vertices; at a nonadjacent second vertex there are no new incident edges. This proves the exact retained hull. The cap's base volume and perpendicular height give normalized volume binom(n-2,k-1) with the stated covolume sqrt(n). Nonadjacent open caps are disjoint by x(H)+x(J)<=k+|H intersection J|. In the adjacent case writing y_a=1-x_a, d=sum y, u=x_i-d, v=x_j-d and z_b=x_b yields nonnegative coordinates of sum 1, and the inverse is integer-affine and satisfies the cube constraints. The relative interior with u,v>0 is nonempty and dense up to the boundary, so the closure of the open overlap is the whole unimodular simplex. Inclusion–exclusion gives the +1 correction. The deleted-vertex foot, equal to 1-1/k on its support and 1/(n-k) off, satisfies both cuts since 1/k+1/(n-k)<=1. Its orthogonal residual has squared norm n/[k(n-k)]. Distance convexity excludes combinations using any retained vertex from the maximizer set; strict Euclidean convexity for the distinct residuals excludes the open segment between the two deleted vertices. The lower-dimensional n=4,k=2 opposite-vertex case correctly gives normalized volume zero and distance one. The supplied hull and determinant scripts were inspected, not executed. One nonblocking bibliographic locator correction: the claimed Ferroni–Schröter formula is Cor. 7.6, §7.1, in the currently retrieved arXiv PDF, not Cor. 6.7, §6.

value.rationale: Two deletions are the first test of interaction between natural vertex caps of the hypersimplex. The overlap is not just a small measured difference: it is a single unimodular cell, and it occurs exactly on the Johnson edges. In contrast the exact worst Euclidean distance and where it occurs do not change, including the dimension-drop regime. This separates two concrete robustness invariants of a canonical polytope and supplies a useful local geometric description beyond generic hull-volume computation.
